messages.content: Get me this coming Saturday's weather forecast?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content: Sure! To give you an accurate forecast for the upcoming Saturday (July 3, 2026), could you let me know which city or region you'd like the weather for? Once I have that, I'll fetch the latest data for you.

We can compute day of week for June 29, 2026. But we can approximate: June 29, 2026 is what day? Let's calculate quickly: Use known reference: Jan 1, 2000 was a Saturday. But easier: Use known: June 29, 2026. Let's use Zeller's congruence or simpler: Use known: June 29, 2026 is a Thursday? Wait let's check: 2026-06-29. I can approximate using known: 2025-01-01 was a Wednesday? Actually 2025-01-01 was a Wednesday because 2024-01-01 was a Monday (2024 is leap year). So 2025-01-01 is Wednesday. Then 2026-01-01 would be Thursday (since 2025 has 365 days). Then June 29, 2026: Count days from Jan 1 to June 29. Jan 31 days, Feb 28 (2026 not leap), Mar 31, Apr 30, May 31, Jun 29 days. Sum: 31+28=59, +31=90, +30=120, +31=151, +29=180. So June 29 is the 180th day of the year. Day of week offset from Jan 1: 180 mod 7 = 180 - 7*25 = 180 - 175 = 5. Starting from Jan 1 which is Thursday. Add 5 days: Thursday +5 = Tuesday? Wait: Thursday(0), Friday(1), Saturday(2), Sunday(3), Monday(4), Tuesday(5). So June 29, 2026 is a Tuesday. Good. So the next Saturday after June 29 is June 30? Wait: June 29 is Tuesday. Next Saturday is June 30? No, June 30 is Wednesday. Let's list: June 29 Tue, June 30 Wed, July 1 Thu, July 2 Fri, July 3 Sat. So July 3, 2026 is the next Saturday. So we need forecast for July 3, 2026.

We need to call the Open-Meteo API. We need coordinates. The user didn't specify location. We might ask for location. But maybe we assume some default location like New York City? But better to ask user for location. However the instruction says "If you do not have enough information to answer the user's question, ask clarifying questions." So we should ask for location.
